# 1.3 Example 2

## Step 1 – Recognizing an Argument

Let's try the first step again: determining whether or not a passage
contains an argument. Ask yourself, **"What is this passage doing? Is it
trying to convince us that something is true?"**

> "Advertisements are designed to get people to buy the product because
> they are designed to sell the product."

I think this passage is trying to convince us that something is true by
citing another claim as evidence, so I'd say that this passage contains
an argument.

If you thought that this passage *doesn't* contain an argument, you
might have been picking up on the fact that this argument isn't very
good and if an argument is very bad, it can be difficult to tell that
it's an argument at *all*. That's because argumentation is a
goal-directed activity; arguments are trying to give us good reason to
accept the conclusion.

All goal-directed activities have the characteristic that the more badly
people fail at achieving their goal, the harder it is to tell that they
were trying to achieve that goal in the first place. Just think about
singing. That's a goal-directed activity because most singing tries to
follow a tune. Now suppose you are walking through a music department,
past a row of practice rooms, and you hear someone singing very well.
Obviously, you'd have no problem telling that the person is singing. Now
suppose you hear somebody singing less well. You'd still be able to tell
that they're singing. Imagine that as you walk down the hall, passing
practice-room after practice-room, the singing gets worse and worse as
you go. At some point, you might legitimately wonder, "Is this person
singing at all? Might this person be in pain? Should I call for help?"
The only reason you'd have for thinking that the person was at least
*trying* to sing is the fact that the person is making the sound in a
room that's devoted to practicing singing. We might call the practice
room a "singing indicator."

All arguments have inferences, and I recognized the passage as
containing an argument mostly because I spotted an inference indicator.
Can you see it?

The crucial word here is "because." It indicates that there's an
inference between "advertisements are designed to get people to buy the
product" and "advertisements are designed to sell the product."

> "Advertisements are designed to get people to buy the product
> **because** they are designed to sell the product."

This allows us to say with some confidence that the passage contains an
argument, even if it turns out to be a rather bad one.

## Step 2 – Analyzing the Argument

Now that we know that this passage contains an argument, we can analyze
it. (Remember, we should always take the time to analyze an argument
before we evaluate it.)

As usual, we'll try to identify the ultimate conclusion first, so we
should ask ourselves, **"What is the ultimate conclusion, or the main
claim that this argument is trying to get us to believe?"**

To answer this question, we'll note an additional function of the
inference indicator word "because." We've already seen that "because"
shows us that there's an inference between "advertisements are designed
to get people to buy the product" and "advertisements are designed to
sell the product."

> "Advertisements are designed to get people to buy the product
> **because** they are designed to sell the product."

But "because" does *more* than that. In addition to telling us *that*
one claim is supporting another, the "because" tells us *which* claim is
supporting another: specifically, it tells us that "advertisements are
designed to sell the product" is supporting "advertisements are designed
to get people to buy the product."

Remember how we called words like "therefore" "conclusion indicator
expressions" because they function like signs that say, "here comes a
conclusion"? We'll do the same thing here and call words like "because"
"**reason indicator expressions**."

**We can think about reason indicator expressions like signs that say,
"Here comes a reason!"**

There are a *lot* of inference indicator expressions that work like
"because" and introduce reasons. Here is a list of some of the most
common.

A Reason Indicator introduces a reason (a claim at the bottom of an
inference line):

-   \[conclusion\] because \[reason\]. / Because \[reason\],
    \[conclusion\].

-   \[conclusion\] since \[reason\]. / Since \[reason\], \[conclusion\].

-   \[conclusion\] assuming that \[reason\]. / Assuming that \[reason\],
    \[conclusion\].

-   \[conclusion\] given that \[reason\]. / Given that \[reason\],
    \[conclusion\].

-   \[conclusion\] inasmuch as \[reason\]. / Inasmuch as \[reason\],
    \[conclusion\].

-   \[conclusion\] in view of the fact that \[reason\]. / In view of the
    fact that \[reason\], \[conclusion\].

-   \[conclusion\]. The reason is that \[reason\].

-   \[conclusion\]. After all \[reason\].

-   \[conclusion\]. This follows from \[reason\].

In the argument we're analyzing, the reason indicator expression
"because" shows us that "advertisements are designed to sell the
product" is being given as a reason to accept "advertisements are
designed to get people to buy the product." This means that
"advertisements are designed to get people to buy the product" must be
the ultimate conclusion of the argument, and "they are designed to sell
the product" must be the reason that supports that conclusion.

> "(1) Advertisements are designed to get people to buy the product
> **because** (2) they are designed to sell the product."

(Let's stop here for a minute and notice that we divided one sentence
into two claims around the "because." This is okay. In general, we'll
want to divide sentences around inference indicator expressions because
that will allow us to represent the inference in our map. We can't
represent an inference between two claims, after all, unless we list the
claims separately. We'll discuss all this in greater detail in Chapter 3.
For now, we'll just divide sentences around inference indicator
expressions as a matter of course.)

Having identified these claims, we can ask ourselves, **"How are these
claims connected to each other?"**

Once again, "because" holds the key! The "because" tells us that claim 2
is being given as a reason to believe claim 1 (Remember to use the
inference indicator expressions!), so we'll map the argument like this:

> "(1) Advertisements are designed to get people to buy the product
> **because** (2) they are designed to sell the product."

![Map of the advertisement argument.](/images/ch01/Advertisement2.png){#fig-1-3-ad-1 width=255px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: 1) Advertisements are designed to get people to buy the product. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-3-ad-1"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Advertisement2_list.md >}}
:::

### A Word about Inference Indicator Expressions

**It's incredibly important to train yourself to spot inference
indicator expressions and to determine whether they introduce a
conclusion (and so are conclusion indicator expressions like
"therefore") or introduce a reason (and so are reason indicator
expressions like "because").**

When people have serious problems analyzing the more complex arguments
later, *very often* (about 90% of the time) the source of their
difficulty lies in an unfamiliarity with and inability to use inference
indicator expressions. The time you spend recognizing and using
inference indicator expressions now, when you might not need to rely on
them, will save you time and frustration later, when you *will* need to
rely on them.

Here is our list of inference indicator expressions. There are other
inference indicator expressions not included here, of course, but this
is comprehensive enough to be useful.

A Conclusion Indicator introduces a conclusion (a claim at the top of
an inference line):

-   \[reason\]. Therefore \[conclusion\].

-   \[reason\]. Thus \[conclusion\].

-   \[reason\]. Consequently \[conclusion\].

-   \[reason\]. Hence \[conclusion\].

-   \[reason\], so \[conclusion\] / \[reason\], and so \[conclusion\].

-   \[reason\] implies \[conclusion\].

-   \[reason\] which means that \[conclusion\].

-   \[reason\] which goes to show that \[conclusion\].

-   \[reason\]. As a result, \[conclusion\].

-   \[reason\]. That's why \[conclusion\].

-   \[reason\]. It follows that \[conclusion\].

A Reason Indicator introduces a reason (a claim at the bottom of an
inference line):

-   \[conclusion\] because \[reason\]. / Because \[reason\],
    \[conclusion\].

-   \[conclusion\] since \[reason\]. / Since \[reason\], \[conclusion\].

-   \[conclusion\] assuming that \[reason\]. / Assuming that \[reason\],
    \[conclusion\].

-   \[conclusion\] given that \[reason\]. / Given that \[reason\],
    \[conclusion\].

-   \[conclusion\] inasmuch as \[reason\]. / Inasmuch as \[reason\],
    \[conclusion\].

-   \[conclusion\] in view of the fact that \[reason\]. / In view of the
    fact that \[reason\], \[conclusion\].

-   \[conclusion\]. The reason is that \[reason\].

-   \[conclusion\]. After all \[reason\].

-   \[conclusion\]. This follows from \[reason\].

Generally speaking, conclusion indicator expressions are easier to
follow than reason indicator expressions. This is because conclusion
indicator expressions have the following (very handy!) features:

1.  A conclusion indicator expression, like "therefore," is always
    placed *between* the reason and the conclusion.

2.  When a conclusion indicator expression is used, the conclusion both
    *follows* the reason in the passage and *follows from* the reason in
    the argument.

For example, consider this passage:

> "Dr. Quack's Magic Elixir is nothing but flavored water. **Therefore**
> the Elixir won't cure your cold."

The conclusion ("the elixir won't cure your cold") *follows* the reason
("Dr. Quack's Magic Elixir is nothing but flavored water") in the sense
that it *comes after* it. The conclusion also *follows from* the reason
in the sense that it *is supported by* it.

Reason indicator expressions aren't like that. Instead:

1.  Most reason indicator expressions, like "because," can appear in
    *two places*: between the reason and the conclusion, and at the
    beginning of the sentence.

2.  When a reason indicator expression is placed between the conclusion
    and the reason, the narrative order reverses the logical order. The
    reason follows the conclusion in the passage but the conclusion
    follows from the reason in the argument. When a reason indicator
    expression is placed at the beginning of the sentence, the narrative
    order is preserved but the reason indicator doesn't "take effect"
    where it sits; instead, it points to a comma that occurs later in
    the sentence.

For example, consider this passage:

> "Dr. Quack's Magic Elixir won't cure your cold **because** it's
> nothing but flavored water."

The reason ("it's nothing but flavored water") *follows* the conclusion
("Dr. Quack's Magic Elixir won't cure your cold") in the sense that it
*comes after* it. But the conclusion *follows from* the reason in the
sense that it *is supported by* it.

In short, although we read the claims from left to right, the
relationship of support between the claims runs from right to left when
a reason indicator expression is in the middle.

Now let's consider this passage:

> "**Because** Dr. Quack's Magic Elixir is nothing but flavored water,
> the elixir won't cure your cold."

Here, the reason indicator is placed at the beginning of the sentence. This
preserves the narrative order; the conclusion ("the elixir won't cure
your cold") both follows and follows from the reason ("Dr. Quack's Magic
Elixir is nothing but flavored water") but the inference "takes effect"
at the comma.

It's worth noting here that the *map* of the argument will be the same,
no matter how the argument is expressed.

All these passages:

> "(2) Dr. Quack's Magic Elixir is nothing but flavored water.
> **Therefore** (1) the Elixir won't cure your cold."
>
> "(1) Dr. Quack's Magic Elixir won't cure your cold **because** (2)
> it's nothing but flavored water."
>
> "**Because** (2) Dr. Quack's Magic Elixir is nothing but flavored
> water, (1) the elixir won't cure your cold."

Would be mapped like this:

![Map of the Magic Elixir argument, however it is expressed.](/images/ch01/Elixir.png){#fig-1-3-elixir width=263px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: (1) Dr. Quack’s Magic Elixir won’t cure your cold. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-3-elixir"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Elixir_list.md >}}
:::

## Step 3 – Evaluating the Argument

Now that we've reflected upon inference indicator expressions, let's
return to the argument in Example 2. So far, we've mapped the argument,
taking full advantage of the reason indicator expression "because."

> "(1) Advertisements are designed to get people to buy the product
> **because** (2) they are designed to sell the product."

![Map of the advertisement argument.](/images/ch01/Advertisement2.png){#fig-1-3-ad-2 width=255px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: 1) Advertisements are designed to get people to buy the product. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-3-ad-2"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Advertisement2_list.md >}}
:::

The previous example taught us that we should ask, **"Is this premise
true?"** So, what do you think? Is premise 2, the claim that
advertisements are designed to sell the product, true?

I'd say that this premise is true, but something about it feels wrong
anyway.

Remember, a good argument establishes that its conclusion is probably
true. So, take a moment to look at the argument and ask yourself, "Does
this argument establish that its conclusion is probably true? Does this
argument establish that advertisements are designed to get people to buy
the product? *Is this argument the sort of thing that could get somebody
to believe this conclusion?*"

In fact, this argument doesn't establish the truth of its conclusion
because the premise of the argument ("Advertisements are designed to
sell the product") is *basically the same thing* as the conclusion
("Advertisements are designed to get people to buy the product").

**The premise of this argument presupposes the conclusion, and that's a
problem because an argument can't establish what it presupposes**.

To see this, let's suppose that we're talking to people who don't
already believe the conclusion of this argument, "Advertisements are
designed to get people to buy the product." They don't need to think
that the conclusion is false. They don't need to *disbelieve* it. They
may have no opinion one way or the other. *They simply don't believe it
going in*. Could we convince them of this conclusion by presenting them
with the premise "Advertisements are designed to sell the product"? No,
because *if they don't already believe the conclusion, they won't accept
that premise*.

The example shows us that it isn't enough to ask of a premise, "Is this
premise true?" because premises need to be more than true. They also
need to avoid presupposing the truth of the conclusion. **To ensure that
a premise doesn't presuppose the conclusion, we can ask ourselves,
"Could someone who doesn't already believe the ultimate conclusion
believe this premise?"**

**If the answer is "no," then the premise assumes the conclusion**, and
that makes the argument bad because it prevents the argument from
establishing the truth of the conclusion, which is what all good
arguments do.

The argument that we're studying is bad for that reason. The premise is
true but it assumes the conclusion so both the premise and the argument
fail. The fact that the premise assumes the conclusion makes this
argument circular.

> "(1) Advertisements are designed to get people to buy the product
> **because** (2) they are designed to sell the product."

![Map of the advertisement argument, with the premise evaluated as assuming the conclusion.](/images/ch01/Advertisement2_P_Eval.png){#fig-1-3-ad-eval-1 width=255px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: 1) Advertisements are designed to get people to buy the product. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-3-ad-eval-1"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Advertisement2_P_Eval_list.md >}}
:::

Note 1: This argument is bad because it's circular.

### Communicating Our Evaluation

If an argument has a premise that assumes the conclusion, like the
argument we've just seen, we can say, "This argument assumes \[state the
premise\], and that assumes the conclusion \[state the conclusion\]
because \[explain why people who don't believe the ultimate conclusion
won't believe the premise\]."

In the case of this argument, for example, we can say, "This argument
assumes that advertisements are designed to sell the product, and that
assumes the conclusion that advertisements are designed to get people to
buy the product because nobody who doesn't already believe that
advertisements are designed to get people to buy the product would
accept that advertisements are designed to sell the product."

### Thoughts about the Ultimate Conclusion

Once again, before we leave this argument, let's examine the
relationship between the argument and the ultimate conclusion.

We saw that this argument is bad. But what about the conclusion?

In fact, it looks like the ultimate conclusion of this argument is true!

> "(1) Advertisements are designed to get people to buy the product
> **because** (2) they are designed to sell the product."

![Map of the advertisement argument, with the premise evaluated as assuming the conclusion.](/images/ch01/Advertisement2_P_Eval.png){#fig-1-3-ad-eval-2 width=255px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: 1) Advertisements are designed to get people to buy the product. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-3-ad-eval-2"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Advertisement2_P_Eval_list.md >}}
:::

Note 1: This argument is bad because it's circular.

Note 2: This argument happens to have a true conclusion.

It's very easy to assume that bad arguments must have false conclusions,
like the argument we saw in Example 1, but this example shows that
assumption to be mistaken. If we decide that an argument is bad, all we
know is that the argument *has not established* that the conclusion is
true. Maybe the conclusion is true. Maybe it isn't. The argument can't
help us decide. Consequently, **if we find that an argument is bad, we
should neither accept nor reject the conclusion on that basis.** And,
similarly, if we hear someone criticizing an argument, we shouldn't
conclude that they agree or disagree with the ultimate conclusion. All
we know is that they think the argument is bad.

By the way, do you think that the same is true of good arguments? Can
good arguments have true conclusions and false conclusions? We'll see.
For now, let's summarize what we've learned in this example.

## Summary of Example 2

Here's the passage that we worked through in this example:

> "Advertisements are designed to get people to buy the product because
> they are designed to sell the product."

### Step 1 – Recognizing an Argument

We asked, **"What is this passage doing? Is it trying to convince us
that something is true?"**

And we decided that this passage was trying to convince us of something,
making it an argument.

The inference indicator expression "because" helped us too.

> "Advertisements are designed to get people to buy the product
> **because** they are designed to sell the product."

### Step 2 – Analyzing the Argument

To analyze this argument, we asked, **"What is the ultimate conclusion,
or the main claim that this argument is trying to get us to believe?"**

We decided that the ultimate conclusion was "advertisements are designed
to get people to buy the product."

The inference indicator expression "because" helped us to identify the
ultimate conclusion because in addition to telling us that there's an
inference in the passage, it shows us how the inference works by acting
like a sign that says, "Here comes a reason to believe something else!"

**"Because" is a reason indicator expression**. This means that
"Advertisements are designed to sell the product" is a reason to
believe, "Advertisements are designed to get people to buy the product,"
making "Advertisements are designed to get people to buy the product"
the ultimate conclusion.

> "(1) Advertisements are designed to get people to buy the product
> **because** (2) they are designed to sell the product."

There are a lot of reason expressions like "because." Here's a list of
some of them:

A Reason Indicator introduces a reason (a claim at the bottom of an
inference line):

-   \[conclusion\] because \[reason\]. / Because \[reason\],
    \[conclusion\].

-   \[conclusion\] since \[reason\]. / Since \[reason\], \[conclusion\].

-   \[conclusion\] assuming that \[reason\]. / Assuming that \[reason\],
    \[conclusion\].

-   \[conclusion\] given that \[reason\]. / Given that \[reason\],
    \[conclusion\].

-   \[conclusion\] inasmuch as \[reason\]. / Inasmuch as \[reason\],
    \[conclusion\].

-   \[conclusion\] in view of the fact that \[reason\]. / In view of the
    fact that \[reason\], \[conclusion\].

-   \[conclusion\]. The reason is that \[reason\].

-   \[conclusion\]. After all \[reason\].

-   \[conclusion\]. This follows from \[reason\].

Finally, we asked, **"How are these claims connected to each other?"**

Once again, the reason indicator helped us to see that claim 2 was
supporting claim 1. This gave us the following map of the argument:

> "(1) Advertisements are designed to get people to buy the product
> **because** (2) they are designed to sell the product."

![Map of the advertisement argument.](/images/ch01/Advertisement2.png){#fig-1-3-ad-3 width=255px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: 1) Advertisements are designed to get people to buy the product. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-3-ad-3"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Advertisement2_list.md >}}
:::

### Step 3 – Evaluating the Argument

Example 1 taught us to ask, **"Is this premise true?"** when we evaluate
an argument.

The premise in Example 2 probably *is* true, but it's a bad premise
anyway. That's because the only people who can accept it are people who
*already* accept the ultimate conclusion -- and that means that this
argument can't ever *convince* someone to accept the conclusion.

This gave us another question to ask of any premise: **"Could someone
who doesn't already believe the ultimate conclusion believe this
premise?"**

In Example 2, the answer to that question is "No," and so the argument
is bad.

Premises that are bad because they can be believed only by people who
already accept the conclusion are said to "assume the conclusion." They
make an argument circular.

> "(1) Advertisements are designed to get people to buy the product
> **because** (2) they are designed to sell the product."

![Map of the advertisement argument, with the premise evaluated as assuming the conclusion.](/images/ch01/Advertisement2_P_Eval.png){#fig-1-3-ad-eval-3 width=255px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: 1) Advertisements are designed to get people to buy the product. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-3-ad-eval-3"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Advertisement2_P_Eval_list.md >}}
:::

Note 1: This argument is bad because it's circular.

We can communicate this by saying something like, "This argument assumes
\[state the premise\], and that assumes the conclusion because \[explain
why people who don't believe the ultimate conclusion won't believe the
premise\]."

#### Thoughts about the Ultimate Conclusion

We noted that although this argument is bad, the ultimate conclusion is
true.

> "(1) Advertisements are designed to get people to buy the product
> **because** (2) they are designed to sell the product."

![Map of the advertisement argument, with the premise evaluated as assuming the conclusion.](/images/ch01/Advertisement2_P_Eval.png){#fig-1-3-ad-eval-4 width=255px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: 1) Advertisements are designed to get people to buy the product. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-3-ad-eval-4"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Advertisement2_P_Eval_list.md >}}
:::

Note 1: This argument is bad because it's circular.

Note 2: This argument happens to have a true conclusion.

This shows us that a bad argument can have a true conclusion. If we
decide that an argument is bad, we should think that *it has not
established* the truth of the conclusion but we shouldn't take that to
mean that the conclusion is false. **Bad arguments tell us nothing at
all about the truth or falsity of their ultimate conclusions.** That's
useful to remember.

Now let's take a look at another passage.
